1. Vide this order, I shall dispose of the present revision petition preferred by Mr. Abhishek Paruthi against order dated 02.06.2022 of Ld.ACMM, South District, whereby the application moved by investigating agency in case FIR No.176/2021 PS Saket for giving direction to him for giving blood sample for DNA Analysis was allowed.
2. Briefly stated, the facts as per the record are as under:-
An FIR bearing no. 176 was lodged in PS Saket on 22.06.2021 for the offences u/s 354/506/509 IPC by the prosecutrix against one Mr. Karan.

During the course of investigation, her statement u/s 164 Cr.P.C. was recorded wherein she was leveled various allegations including that of rape against revisionist so the relevant sections pertaining to that were added.
During the proceedings subsequent thereto, the revisionist was granted bail by Ld. ASJ (South) vide order dated 21.04.2022.

Subsequently, an application dated 21.04.2022 was moved by IO before Ld. ACMM requesting for directions to the revisionist for giving blood sample for the purpose of DNA analysis with that of prosecutrix and of the child given birth by the prosecutrix in October, 2020.

Said application was allowed by Ld. ACMM vide impugned order Abhishek Paruthi vs The State (Nct Of Delhi) on 19 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124673250/
1 and that order is being challenged in these proceedings.

sentences.text: 3. Arguments heard.

The revisionist has assailed the impugned order on three main grounds:-
(i) Ld. Magistrate was not having power to pass the direction to him for giving blood sample by way of allowing application moved by investigating agency as there is no such provision in Cr.P.C.
( ii )
The child has taken birth within 280 days of dissolution of marriage of the prosecutrix so the bar u/s 112 Indian Evidence Act will apply and no evidence can be brought on record to prove otherwise.
(iii) The application of the investigation agency has been disposed by Ld. ACMM by way of non speaking order as no reason thereof has been mentioned in the order.
4. It was argued by Ld. Counsel for revisionist that the present case is a prefect example of abuse of process of law.

It was submitted that the FIR in question was initially registered for the offences u/s 354/506/509 IPC against the brother of the revisionist and it was mentioned in the FIR that the prosecutrix had gone from her house to the revisionist for his help and for saving her life.

Subsequently, for the reasons best known to her, in the statement u/s 164 Cr.P.C., she leveled various allegations including that of rape against the revisionist whereupon the sections pertaining to that were added and investigation was carried out.
It was argued that it is not clear as to how the investigation agency could have mentioned the sections pertaining to rape in the present FIR when the initial FIR was complete in all respects.

It was further argued that there was no provision in the Cr.P.C. empowering the Magistrate to give directions to accused to give his blood sample for matching the DNA with the child who was given birth by the prosecutrix.

It was submitted by him that section 53 and 53A Cr.P.C. provide for a situation when the blood/semens etc. from the accused is to be matched with the material found on the spot of crime or on the body/clothes of the prosecutrix which is not the case here.

So, Ld. Magistrate was not having power to grant the relief as prayed for by the investigating agency and Ld.ACMM has simply written in the impugned order that there is no bar under the law for passing the directions to the accused for giving blood sample for DNA analysis which is not correct approach.

Moving further, it was also argued by Ld. Counsel for revisionist that there is complete bar u/s 112 Indian Evidence Act on matching the DNA of the revisionist with that of the child because admittedly, the prosecutrix was married at the time of commission of alleged rape by revisionist and the child took birth within 280 days of the dissolution of marriage so it is conclusive proof that the child was begotten from the marriage as no proof has come on record to show that her husband has no excess to her during that period.
It was submitted that the attempt by the investigating agency is to question the legitimacy of the child which is not tenable in law.

Ld. Counsel has also moved an application for appointing someone to protect the interest of the child as according to him the interest of the prosecutrix is diametrically opposite to the interest of the child.

Lastly, it was argued that the Ld. ACMM vide impugned order while allowing the application has not dealt with his arguments and has passed a cryptic non speaking Abhishek Paruthi vs The State (Nct Of Delhi) on 19 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124673250/

sentences.text: I have considered the submissions from both the sides alongwith record and the judgments cited.

One of the grounds taken by the revisionist to assail the impugned order is that Ld. Magistrate could not have passed such an order as there was no provision to that effect in Cr.P.C. or any other law.

It was argued by Ld. Counsel for revisionist that the power u/s 53 and 53 A Cr.P.C. is only for those cases where blood samples/semen etc. is to be matched with material found on the spot of crime or on the body/clothes of the prosecutrix which is not the case here.
It was stated that in the absence of any such power, Ld. Magistrate could not have passed the order in question.

8. Section 53 Cr.P.C. provides as under:-
Abhishek Paruthi vs The State (Nct Of Delhi) on 19 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124673250/
4 Section 53. Examination of accused by medical practitioner at the request of police officer.-

entities.text: Abhishek Paruthi vs The State (Nct Of Delhi)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: (1) When a person is arrested on a charge of committing an offence of such a nature and alleged to have committed under such circumstances that there are reasonable grounds for believing that an examination of his person will afford evidence as to the commission of an offence, it shall be lawful for a registered medical practitioner, acting at the request of a police officer not below the ran of sub-inspector, and for any person acting in good faith in his aid and under his direction, to make such an examination of the person arrested as is reasonable necessary in order to ascertain the facts which may afford such evidence, and to use such force as is reasonably necessary for that purpose.

(2) Whenever the person of a female is to be examined under this section, the examination shall be made only by,
or under the supervision of, a female registered medical practitioner.
[Explanation.-

In this section and in sections 53A and 54,-
(a) "examination" shall include the examination of blood, blood stains, semen, swabs in case of sexual offences, sputum and sweat, hair samples and finger nail clippings by the use of modern and scientific techniques including DNA profiling and such other tests which the registered medical practitioner thinks necessary in a particular case;

(b) "registered medical practitioner" means a medical practitioner who possess any medical qualification as defined in clause (h) of the section 2 of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 (102 of 1956) and whose name has been entered in a State Medical Register.]
9. Section 53A Cr.P.C. provides as under:-
[Section 53A. Examination of person accused of rape by medical practitioner.- (1)
When a person is arrested on a charge of committing an offence of rape or an attempt to commit rape and there are reasonable grounds for believing that an examination of his person will afford evidence as to the commission of such offence, it shall be lawful for a registered medical practitioner employed in a hospital run by the Government or by a local authority and in the absence of such a practitioner within the radius of sixteen kilometeres from the place where the offence has been committed by any other registered medical practitioner acting at the request of a police officer not below the rank of a sub-inspector, and for any person acting in good faith in his aid and under his direction, to make such an examination of the arrested person and to use such force as is reasonably necessary for that purpose.

(2) The registered medical practitioner conducting such examination shall without delay, examine such person and prepare a report of his examination giving the following particulars, namely:-
(i) the name and address of the accused and of the person by whom he was brought,
(ii) the age of the accused,

(iii) marks of injury, if any, on the person of the accused,
(iv) the description of material taken from the person of the accused for DNA profiling, and (v) other material particular in reasonable detail.
(3)The report shall state precisely the reasons for each conclusion arrived at.
(4) The exact time of commencement and completion of the examination shall also noted in the report.

(5) The registered medical practitioner shall, without delay, forward the report of the investigating officer, who shall forward it to the Magistrate referred to in section 173 as part of the documents referred to in clause (a) of sub- section (5) of that section.]
10. This Court is unable to see anything in the aforementioned provisions of law thereby limiting its scope to the cases as urged by Ld. Defence Counsel.
No judicial precedent giving such an interpretation to said provisions has been cited.

On the other hand, such a course of action (for taking blood samples of an accused in rape case for DNA examination with prosecutrix and child)
was approved by Hon'ble Kerla High Court in Das @ Anu Vs. State of Kerala (Crl. MC No. 8065 of 2018) and Hon'ble Madras High Court in M. Muthukumar Vs. The Inspector of Police, All Women Police Station, Sivagangai and Ors. Crl. OP (MD) No. 6279 of 2017.

sentences.text: Both these judgments were relied upon by Ld. Counsel for the prosecutrix.
11. In fact, in M. Muthukumar (supra) the accused was on bail like in the present matter.

One of the grounds taken for challenging the order of Ld. Trial Court allowing the application of the investigating agency for direction to accused to give his blood sample for his DNA test alongwith that of prosecutrix and the child, was that u/s 53 and 53A of Cr.P.C., an accused who has been arrested on charge of committing rape can be subjected to DNA test, however, in that case, the accused had obtained anticipatory bail and therefore, was not arrested.
It was argued that in view of that, the police was not having power to invoke Section 53 and 53A Cr.P.C.
Said argument was dealt with by Hon'ble High Court in following manner:-

The first ground raised by the learned Counsel for the petitioner is that Section 53 and 53A of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be put into operation, only when a person is arrested on the charge of committing an offence of a rape and since the petitioner has obtained an anticipatory bail, the said provision cannot be applied to the petitioner.
This Court is not in agreement of this submission.
A person released on bail is still considered to be detained in the constructive custody of the Court through his surety.
He is notionally in the custody of the Court and hence continues to be a person arrested.

In spite of the fact that the accused person has been released on bail, he continues to be a person arrested on charge of commission of an offence Abhishek Paruthi vs The State (Nct Of Delhi) on 19 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124673250/
6 and, therefore, his medical examination can be carried out.

entities.text: Abhishek Paruthi vs The State (Nct Of Delhi)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In other words, the release of an arrested person on bail or a person who has obtained anticipatory bail surrenders before the Court, cannot take away the reality of the situation and he does not seize to be an arrested person or an accused person for the purpose of Section 53 and 53A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

12. In this case also, it appears that the application was moved before Ld. Magistrate as the revisionist was on bail at that time otherwise the investigating officer herself was competent to request a medical practitioner to do the needful.
So, this Court is of the view that Ld. Magistrate was well within its power to allow the application moved by IO and the impugned order cannot be faulted with on this ground.

13. Second ground taken by Ld. Counsel for revisionist is that in view of Section 112, Indian Evidence Act, 1872 directing the revisionist to give blood samples so as to check the paternity of the child is impermissible.

For appreciating said line of reasoning, it will be appropriate to reproduce Section 112, Indian Evidence Act below:-
S.112. Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy.- The fact that any person was born during the continuance of a valid marriage between his mother and any man, or within two hundred and eighty days after its dissolution, the mother remaining unmarried, shall be conclusive proof that he is the legitimate son of that man, unless it can be shown that the parties to the marriage and no access to each other at any time when he could have been begotten.

14. Now, some undisputed facts are worth mentioning (the child is being referred to as 'A' in the subsequent portion of this order):-
a. 'A' was born in October, 2021.
b.
The FIR in question was lodged on 22.06.2021 and allegations of rape against the revisionist were leveled later on in the statement u/s 164 Cr.P.C. of the prosecutrix.

c. At the time, when 'A' could have been conceived, the prosecutrix was legally married (although it has been submitted on her behalf that she was living separately from her husband since February,
2018 till her divorce in April 2021).

d. The allegations are pertaining to alleged sexual relationship between the parties wherein both of them were married and the prosecutrix was allegedly made to believe that revisionist was in love with her.

15. Now, this Court shall seek guidance from the judgments of Hon'ble Apex Court regarding the import of Section 112, Indian Evidence Act in such facts and the circumstances in which said provision can be ignored.

sentences.text: In that case, an FIR was registered by the prosecutrix against her husband and brother-in-law (husband's brother) for the offences u/s 498A/323/354/506/509 IPC and chargesheet was filed after completion of investigation.

During trial after several witnesses were examined, prosecutrix moved an application u/s 45 of the Indian Evidence Act with prayer for direction for obtaining expert opinion for DNA fingerprint test comparing blood samples of her two minor daughters with that of her brother-in-law.
The allegations were that she was forced to develop physical relations with him and the children were born out of that relationship.

The Trial Court allowed the application whereupon revision petition was filed before Hon'ble High Court of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh by her husband and brother-in- law but same was dismissed holding that DNA fingerprint test was permitted u/s 53,53A and 54 of the Cr.P.C.

sentences.text: An SLP was filed against said order before Hon'ble Apex Court.
Hon'ble Court quoted with approval following portion from the Judgment of a coordinate Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ashok Kumar Vs. Raj Gupta and Ors.

entities.text: Ashok Kumar Vs. Raj Gupta and Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: DNA is unique to an individual (barring twins) and can be used to identify a person's identity, trace familial linkages or even reveal sensitive health information.

Whether a person can be compelled to provide a sample for DNA in such matters can also be answered considering the test of proportionality laid down in the unanimous decision of this Court in K.S.Puttaswamy (Aadhaar5 J.) V. Union of India [K.S.Puttaswamy (Aadhaar-5 J.) Vs. Union of India, (2019) 1 SCC 1], wherein the right to privacy has been declared a constitutionally protected right in India.

entities.text: K.S.Puttaswamy (Aadhaar5 J.) V. Union of India [K.S.Puttaswamy (Aadhaar-5 J.) Vs. Union of India, (2019) 1 SCC 1]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Court should therefore examine the proportionality of the legitimate aims being pursued i.e. whether the same are not arbitrary or discriminatory, whether they may have an adverse impact on the person and that they justify the encroachment upon the privacy and personal autonomy of the person, being subjected to the DNA test.
(emphasis supplied)

17. Thereafter, Hon'ble Apex Court decided the said SLP by holding as under:-
6.
In the present proceedings, we are taking two factors into account which have been ignored by the Trial Court as also the Revisional Court.
The Trial Court allowed the application of the respondent no.2 mechanically, on the premise that the DNA fingerprint test is permissible under the law.

High Court has also proceeded on the basis, referring to different authorities including the case of Dipanwita Roy V.
Ronobroto Roy [2015 (1) SCC 365].

entities.text:
Dipanwita Roy V.
Ronobroto Roy [2015 (1) SCC 365]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The ratio of the case was also examined by the Coordinate Bench in the decision of the Ashok Kumar (supra).
7.

The first factor, which,in our opinion, is of significance, is that in the judgment under appeal, blood sampling of the children was directed, who were not parties to the proceeding nor were their status required to be examined in the complaint of the respondent no.2.

This raised doubt on their legitimacy of being borne to legally Abhishek Paruthi vs The State (Nct Of Delhi) on 19 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/124673250/
8

entities.text: Abhishek Paruthi vs The State (Nct Of Delhi)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: wedded parents and such directions,if carried out, have the potential of exposing them to inheritance related complication.
Section 112 of the Evidence Act, also gives a protective cover from allegations of this nature.

The said provision stipulates:-
"Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy.-

The fact that any person was born during the continuance of a valid marriage between his mother and any man, or within two hundred and eighty days after its dissolution, the mother remaining unmarried, shall be conclusive proof that he is he legitimate son of that man, unless it can be shown that the parties to the marriage had no access to each other at any time when he could have been begotten."
8.
In our opinion, the Trial Court as also the Revisional Court had completely ignored the said factor and proceeded as if the children were material objects who could be sent for forensic analysis.
The other factor, in our opinion, which was ignored by the said two Courts is that the paternity of the children was not in question in the subject-proceeding.

9. The substance of the complaint was not related to paternity of the children of the respondent no.2 but the question was whether of the offences under the aforesaid provisions of the 1860 Code was committed against her or not.
The paternity of the two daughters of the respondent no.2 is collateral factor to the allegations on which the criminal case in otherwise founded.
On the basis of the available materials, in our opinion,the case out of which this proceeding arises could be decided without considering the DNA test report.
This as the reasoning which was considered by the Coordinate Bench in the case of Ashok Kumar (supra), though that was a civil suit.

Merely because something is permissible under the law cannot be directed as a matter of course to be performed particularly when a direction to that effect would be invasive to the physical autonomy of a person.
The consequence thereof would not be confined to the question as to whether such an order would result in testimonial compulsion,but encompasses right to privacy as well.

Such direction would violate the privacy right of the persons subject to such tests and could be prejudicial to the future of the two children who were also sought to be brought within the ambit of the Trial Court's direction.
(emphasis supplied)

18. Similar was the decision of Hon'ble Apex Court in another judgment relating to interpretation of import of Section 112, Indian Evidence Act, although in somewhat different facts, in Aparna Ajinkya Firodia Vs. Ajinkya Arun Firodia, Civil Appeal No..of 2023 dated 20.02.2023.

sentences.text: Both the judgments quoted above have been relied upon by Ld. Counsel for the revisionist.
The prosecutrix has also relied upon 23 judgments in support of her case, however, none of those judgments deals with the question before this Court in the present matter.
In none of those judgments, the import of Section 112, Indian Evidence Act, 1872 has been dealt with, so same are of no help to the case of prosecution/prosecutrix on this point.
20. As mentioned earlier, the prosecutrix was married at the time when 'A' could have been conceived.

Although, she has stated that she was living separately from her husband for last around three years at that time, however, such a separation between the parties has not been treated as an exception to Section 112, Indian Evidence Act.
In fact only exception provided is, in case, it can be shown that parties to the marriage had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten.

Ld. Counsel for prosecutrix had submitted that she alongwith her husband had mentioned in their mutual divorce petition supported with their respective affidavits that they were living separately since 2018 and that they did not have access to each other during that time.

In view of this Court, mentioning of this fact in the mutual divorce petition supported with the affidavits of both the parties is not sufficient to prove the important fact that they both did not have access to each other.
The conclusive proof as mentioned in Section 112, Indian Evidence Act cannot be displaced by such a weak piece of evidence.
Admittedly, there is no other material with the investigating agency or at least, no such material has been cited before this Court to show the factum of non-access.

21. This Court is conscious of the fact that by way of present revision petition, the Court is dealing with an aspect of investigation pertaining to offence of rape which is indisputably a heinous offence against a woman, however, merely the gravity of the offence cannot be the sole guide in deciding the present petition because it involves the valuable rights of 'A' which cannot be brushed aside lightly due to sexual misadventures of the parties.
The innocent child cannot be used as a tool by the prosecution in its quest to collect evidence against the revisionist.

The following paragraph from the judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court in Aparna Ajinkya Firodia (supra), is worth quoting as it sums up the consequences which might have to be faced by 'A', if DNA test is allowed in the present matter:-
23.
'Illegitimate'- a term that brands an individual with the shame of being born outside wedlock, casts a shadow on one's identity.

Times change and attitudes may change, but the impact of growing up with the social stigma of being illegitimate,
does not.

The Courts must hence be inclined towards upholding the legitimacy of the child unless the facts are so compulsive and clinching as to necessarily warrant a finding that the child could at all have been begotten to the father and as such a legitimisation of the child would result in rank injustice to the father, vide Dukhtar Jahan Vs. Mohammed Farooq, (1987) 1 SCC 624.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
A person released on bail is still considered to be detained in the constructive custody of the Court through his surety.
In other words, the release of an arrested person on bail or a person who has obtained anticipatory bail surrenders before the Court, cannot take away the reality of the situation and he does not seize to be an arrested person or an accused person for the purpose of Section 53 and 53A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Whether a person can be compelled to provide a sample for DNA in such matters can also be answered considering the test of proportionality laid down in the unanimous decision of this Court in K.S.Puttaswamy (Aadhaar5 J.) V. Union of India [K.S.Puttaswamy (Aadhaar-5 J.) Vs. Union of India, (2019) 1 SCC 1], wherein the right to privacy has been declared a constitutionally protected right in India.
The Court should therefore examine the proportionality of the legitimate aims being pursued i.e. whether the same are not arbitrary or discriminatory, whether they may have an adverse impact on the person and that they justify the encroachment upon the privacy and personal autonomy of the person, being subjected to the DNA test.
The Trial Court allowed the application of the respondent no.2 mechanically, on the premise that the DNA fingerprint test is permissible under the law.
High Court has also proceeded on the basis, referring to different authorities including the case of Dipanwita Roy V.
Ronobroto Roy [2015 (1) SCC 365].
The paternity of the two daughters of the respondent no.2 is collateral factor to the allegations on which the criminal case in otherwise founded.
Merely because something is permissible under the law cannot be directed as a matter of course to be performed particularly when a direction to that effect would be invasive to the physical autonomy of a person.
The consequence thereof would not be confined to the question as to whether such an order would result in testimonial compulsion,but encompasses right to privacy as well.
Such direction would violate the privacy right of the persons subject to such tests and could be prejudicial to the future of the two children who were also sought to be brought within the ambit of the Trial Court's direction.
Further, a direction to conduct DNA test of a child, is to be ordered even rarely, in cases where the paternity of a child is not directly in issue but is merely collateral to the proceeding, such as in the instant case.
Although, she has stated that she was living separately from her husband for last around three years at that time, however, such a separation between the parties has not been treated as an exception to Section 112, Indian Evidence Act.
In fact only exception provided is, in case, it can be shown that parties to the marriage had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten.
The conclusive proof as mentioned in Section 112, Indian Evidence Act cannot be displaced by such a weak piece of evidence.
Admittedly, there is no other material with the investigating agency or at least, no such material has been cited before this Court to show the factum of non-access.
21. This Court is conscious of the fact that by way of present revision petition, the Court is dealing with an aspect of investigation pertaining to offence of rape which is indisputably a heinous offence against a woman, however, merely the gravity of the offence cannot be the sole guide in deciding the present petition because it involves the valuable rights of 'A' which cannot be brushed aside lightly due to sexual misadventures of the parties.
The innocent child cannot be used as a tool by the prosecution in its quest to collect evidence against the revisionist.
'Illegitimate'- a term that brands an individual with the shame of being born outside wedlock, casts a shadow on one's identity.
Times change and attitudes may change, but the impact of growing up with the social stigma of being illegitimate,
does not.
The Courts must hence be inclined towards upholding the legitimacy of the child unless the facts are so compulsive and clinching as to necessarily warrant a finding that the child could at all have been begotten to the father and as such a legitimisation of the child would result in rank injustice to the father, vide Dukhtar Jahan Vs. Mohammed Farooq, (1987) 1 SCC 624.
22.
Considering the above discussion, this Court is of the firm view that the application moved on behalf of investigating agency could not have been allowed as it will necessarily involve the issue of "legitimacy" of 'A' which is not absolutely essential for proving the alleged offence.
The offence in question can be proved by other material including the oral testimony of the prosecutrix.
